newsitem.title: USA: USDA to hold meetings on interstate meat issue.
newsitem.headline: USDA to hold meetings on interstate meat issue.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department's Food and Safety Inspection Service (FSIS) said Friday it would hold two public meetings on the long-running issue of whether to permit interstate shipment of state-inspected meat and poultry.
FSIS said the meetings would take place in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, on June 16 and in Washington, D.C., on June 19.
"FSIS is conducting these meetings to assist USDA in determining what additional steps are needed to resolve the interstate commerce issue," FSIS administrator Thomas Billy said in a statement.
Currently, only federally-inspected meat and poultry products may be sold across state lines.
Some state-inspected meat companies have been pressing USDA to allow them to sell their products in other states without federal inspection.
Last month, the Ohio Department of Agriculture, together with three Ohio meat packing companies and the Ohio Association of Meat Processors, sued USDA to overturn the law.
They argued that federal law already requires all state meat and poultry inspection programs to be "at least equal to" federal standards.
Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman recently told a meeting of state agriculture directors that he understood their concerns but did not want to risk losing public trust in food safety.

"Philosophically, I would like to see us move toward allowing state inspections but we're not there yet," Glickman said. New meat inspection rules requiring scientific testing for disease-cause bacteria needed to get into full swing first, he said.

The American Meat Insitute, which represents meat packers, opposes the idea, saying the overwhelming majority of its members prefer one uniform federal inspection program for products shipped across state lines or in international trade.
